Mr. Speaker, before this session is concluded there is one piece of legislation which I believe the government should implement; I refer to Bill No. 135, which was passed last year, amending the wheat board act to enable coarse grains to be marketed through the wheat board. Hon. members will recall that last year, when this legislation was before the house, evidence was given that both the farmers who were using the coarse grains in eastern Canada, and the farmers in western Canada who were producing those coarse

Coarse Grains
grains, desired the grain to be marketed through the wheat board.
Pressure was put on the government here to pass the necessary legislation. That legislation was introduced in the form of Bill No. 135. When the bill was passed, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) insisted that complementary legislation should be passed by the provinces before the act would be implemented. On page 2422 of last year's Hansard he stated this:
I repeat that our powers are not sufficient, and this bill is not sufficient, to organize a compulsory pool on wheat and barley that would succeed. What others do is the responsibility of others.
It may be that we shall have sufficient legislation passed in those proper jurisdictions to enable the pool to be worked out. If that is so, the government has done its part, and will be ready to act.
The minister's statement is definite that when complementary legislation was passed in the three prairie provinces, this government would be prepared to implement the act. Such complementary legislation has now been passed. It was passed unanimously a year ago by the Saskatchewan government. It was passed early this session by the Alberta government, I believe unanimously. It was passed recently by the Manitoba government, by a vote of thirty-six to twelve, practically all the rural members voting for the bill.
In answer to a question raised by the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) on April 25, the minister stated:
The government set the prerequisite to the act being brought into force on two or three occasions. Apparently that prerequisite has been complied with. The government will study the situation in the light of what has been said in the past.
What was definitely said was that this legislation would be implemented when the provinces agreed to it; that was the prerequisite, and it has been met. I believe that this government should now, before the conclusion of this session, give notice that this legislation is being implemented, and announce the price that will be paid for oats and barley for the coming year.
The minister agrees that we should have greater production of coarse grains. In answer to a further question I asked on April 25, the minister stated this:
Speaking as the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I hope there will be a great deal of coarse grain sown this year. I can say again that the government will give consideration to the matter in the hope of making an early announcement.
I am sorry that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not in Canada at the present time. I understand he is in the old country on business which I believe is connected with the marketing of our products in Great Britain. What is the position in that regard? In 1944 we reached the peak in the marketing of our agricultural products in Great Britain.

In that year we shipped to Great Britain over 719 million pounds of pork products; this year our contract with Great Britain for bacon is for 160 million pounds. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) recently stated that he doubted whether we could supply that quantity. Why can we not supply it? The Minister of Agriculture has told this house time and time again that the production of dairy products and of meat products in this country depends primarily on the production of coarse grains. It is only when we have coarse grains to feed that we can increase our production of these products. Many people in this country are blaming Great Britain for not buying more Canadian products. How can we expect Great Britain to enter into contracts with Canada for these products when we cannot supply them?
There are two things which Great Britain demands of those who supply her with her food. One thing is continuity of supply. She wants to know that she is going to be able to get certain quantities of these products from year to year-not only this year but next year and two, three, four or five years from now. She wants to know that she can depend on that supply. How can she depend upon Canada when our production varies to the extent that it does?
Another thing that she demands is uniform quality. The Britisher likes to go down to the shop and to be able to buy his bacon or his cheese today, next week or next year and know that it is going to be the same quality. That quality can only be maintained by export boards in this country which will maintain the continuity and the uniformity of our exports. The first step towards that end is in securing an adequate supply of coarse grains for feed in this country. What is the position with respect to grains in western Canada or what will be the position? Under the world wheat agreement we have a sale for wheat of approximately 203 million bushels. Our average production of wheat over a number of years has been considerably over that figure. It has been something like an average of 280 million bushels a year. If we have a sale for only 203 million bushels and if we do not find other markets, it simply means that we shall get a surplus in this country and we shall be back on a quota with regard to the production of wheat.
In determining what he is going to sow, the farmer in western Canada takes into consideration two or three things. He takes into consideration the weather, the type of land he is sowing and the price of the grain that he may be sowing. A rough rule of thumb with regard to prices that is used by most farmers is this. If oats are selling at less than half the price of wheat, it pays

better to sow wheat. If barley is selling at less than two-thirds the price of wheat, the farmer prefers to sow wheat rather than barley, provided weather conditions are favourable and his soil is suitable. This year we have a guaranteed price for wheat of $1.75 per bushel. That is the floor under wheat. The floor under oats is 61'J cents and the floor under barley is 90 cents-approximately one-third for oats and one-half for barley. Naturally unless the government implement this legislation and give some idea of what the prices of coarse grains are going to be, the result is going to be that there will be from two million to three million more acres sown to wheat in western Canada this year than were sown last year. That situation will result in a surplus, with the result that we shall be unable to fulfil even our reduced contracts to Great Britain with respect to bacon, cheese and eggs.
I think that the government should immediately make an announcement stating that they have implemented Bill No. 135 and stating the price that they are going to be prepared to pay for oats and barley in the coming year. Unless that is done I feel quite sure that the result will be reduced sowings of coarse grains and reduced production of these products which should be the basis of mixed agriculture in western Canada.
The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) announced that the subsidy on coarse grains was going to be continued after July 31 this year. One of the things which reduced the production of bacon and dairy products in western Canada is the fact that the government were prepared to subsidize the freight on coarse grains while they failed to subsidize the finished product produced in western Canada to the amount of the freight to eastern Canada. Until this government decides to give more consideration to some of these matters, I am afraid that we shall lose our contracts with Great Britain, that we shall not be able to fulfil them, and that we shall destroy the agricultural industry in western Canada.
I want to urge just as strongly as I can that the government give immediate consideration to implementing Bill No. 135, stating the price that they will be prepared to pay under that bill for oats and barley in the coming year.

Even at this late time in the session I believe that the importance of the subject, to which I should like to direct the attention of the house for a few moments, justifies its inclusion in our discussion. I have reference to the matter of the trans-Canada highway route across the four provinces of western Canada. There are members in the house who will recall that on July 11, 1947, as recorded at page 5460 of Hansard, I raised this question for discussion, and was joined by a number of hon. members. The members for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum), Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), Weyburn (Mr. McKay), Swift Current (Mr. Bentley), Macleod (Mr. Hansell), Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), Kootenay East (Mr. Matthews), Regina City (Mr. Probe), and others, spoke in favour of the southernmost route for the trans-Canada highway. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine), the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald) and other hon. members spoke in favour of the Yellowhead route. The points brought forward at that time I thought justified most careful consideration by the government of all matters pertaining to a trans-Canada highway.
At that time there were in the public mind three possible routes, namely the Yellowhead 09087-170J
Trans-Canada Highway route, or the Evergreen highway, running from Brandon to Saskatoon and Edmonton, through the Yellowhead pass to Kamloops, Hope and Vancouver. The central route ran from Brandon to Medicine Hat and Calgary, through the Kicking Horse pass to Hope and Vancouver. The southernmost route ran from Brandon to Medicine Hat and Lethbridge, then through the Crowsnest pass to Trail, Hope and Vancouver.
Since our discussions in 1947 a tremendous amount of interest has been developed throughout western Canada, and eastern Canada as well, and the government has given the matter considerable attention. One or two conferences have been held. Since that time, too, there has been an extremely rapid growth in several other respects throughout Canada. Oil developments in Alberta and other parts of Canada have been in proportions altogether unexpected, as regards their extent and richness. The possibility of developing our own steel and iron, and heavy industries in Canada, has been visualized as never before. The development of irrigation has been talked about and promised as never before, all through Alberta and Saskatchewan. There has been a kindling of national consciousness and a confidence such as we have never had before. We have come to have a: greater respect for the provinces, owing in large measure I believe to a wise change of attitude on the part of the government at Ottawa. We have had a renewed appreciation of the British commonwealth, as opposed to internationalism. In 1947 a great many people could not mention the United Nations, Bretton Woods, and all the rest of those organizations, without having day dreams. But now they are getting down pretty close to realities, and they are coming to the conclusion that the British commonwealth is a pretty good organization to be a part of.
If we look to the British commonwealth in any large measure for our safety in peace and in war it becomes necessary that we in Canada reorient our development in some measure with the British commonwealth in mind, as well as the United States. There has developed an enhanced realization of Canada's strategic importance in the British commonwealth of nations. All these matters have an important bearing on the necessity of developing at an early stage an adequate highway system throughout western Canada.
Up to the present time the interest of the various areas in developing the highway through their particular portions of Canada has been all to the good, because it has impressed upon the people as a whole the necessity for a trans-Canada highway. I hope this excitement does not go too far, because if it does we shall see a tendency for the various areas to nullify each other's efforts.

This is the amount of money that Alberta has been spending on roads generally during the last few years: In 1945-46 it amounted to $4,500,000; in 1946-47, $7,300,000; in 1947-48, $12 million. Those figures are only approximate, but they are substantially correct.
This will serve to show the members of the house that the province of Alberta is in no way neglecting her share in the building of highways, all of which will benefit Canada. I do not believe there is any necessity to point out to the members of the house that any development which takes place in any one province is an asset to the whole dominion. Especially is that the case in respect to roads when man travels so far and so fast all over this country.

I do not wish to put any block in the way of the other two highway routes or any other route that might be considered valuable. I should like however to leave with the house, and with the government, some suggestion of the reasons for the urgency in building the southernmost route of the trans-Canada highway. This route will pass through the most densely populated area in the provinces concerned. It will pass through the largest tax-producing area. It will pass through an area very important for farming, oil development, lumbering, fruit growing, mining and smelting, seed producing, sugar producing, parks and tourists' attractions. It is the most direct route from Winnipeg west to Vancouver. It is an all-weather route. It is the nearest route to the United States.
Owing to the fact that it is the nearest route to the United States, I think it is of the utmost importance that this route be finished first. I may be quite wrong, and my friends from other areas might disagree with me, but generally speaking we find that if you can get United States tourists inside this country and over the first one hundred miles, they take courage and probe further into the depths of Canada.
If we were to build the Yellowhead route, for example, and people were to enter Canada, let us say around Carway, which is near the Waterton lakes park, they would come in contact with nothing but just the gravel and they would never get up where they could use the Yellowhead pass route. On the contrary, if we could get this southernmost route built for all Canada to take pride in it. then we would stand a fine chance of getting many United States tourists to come into Canada. They would take heart and go far into the hinterland of the north. Remember that the Alaska highway would be reached before long from this southernmost highway.
There are upwards of forty connecting points of entry to the United States between Winnipeg and Vancouver, which strengthens what I am saying concerning this southern route. This route is the natural inlet to Canada's national parks. I do not think it would be advisable for me to take the time to name those parks. I shall simply refer to two in western Canada, namely, the Water-ton lakes park in my own constituency, and Banff national park which is well-known all over Canada, both easily accessible from the southern route.
Mr. Speaker. I think I have burdened the house long enough in connection with this matter. I have no desire to hold up the progress of the house at this time-

I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question. Has he studied the
Trans-Canada Highway population of the western provinces in relation to the various proposed routes? Is it not quite true that the majority of the people in those provinces live north of the proposed Yellowhead line?

No doubt that is true; I am not in a position to say offhand. May I tell the member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine)-I honour him for sticking up for his area in Alberta-that I am dependent for the information I have just given upon the pamphlet "Highlights of the Southern Trans-Canada Highway; an all-year short route", issued by the Southern Trans-Canada Highway Association. I think it will be found that that organization is very dependable.
But somewhat prejudiced.

Just as the organizations for each of the other routes are somewhat prejudiced. I think we can depend upon the statements which I gave to the effect that the population along the proposed southern route is the most dense.
I believe that, very dense.

I do not know if the existence of the majority of the population north of the Yellowhead pass route would have any special bearing. They might be so far from the Yellowhead pass route that they could reach it only by boat. After all, what we must consider in contemplating the development of a highway, in relation to the people through whose area it is to pass, is the number of people who will be served immediately by that highway. When you consider the question from that aspect I am quite sure there is no doubt that there are more people along the southern route than along either of the other proposed routes.
May I repeat one remark before I close? I have no desire to concentrate the attention of the government on one of these highways excluding the others. All three of them are highly desirable and the three of them must be built within as short a time as possible. I believe each of them is exceedingly important strategically. At the same time, I think what I have said is sound.
While I am in favour of the development of a highway system, I think some one of these highways has to be developed first. I believe that, all things being considered, we should construct the southern route first.
I am interested in seeing that plenty of dominion money is made available. Some may say that a billion dollars is too much money for the government to spend on a highway system. I do not believe that. I believe that a billion dollars spent on a highway, in co-operation with the provinces, would be money well spent. I believe any

administration would be able to look back with pride on the expenditure of that money. After a few years they would find it easy, even unnecessary, to defend it.
I suggest that we spend enough money to build the highways and that the dominion ask all the provinces to plan the most desirable highways. Then we should build those highways without delay.

I should like to state very briefly what seems to me to be the substance of the proposal which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has submitted today. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1949, for the purposes of the government, this house voted $2,190 million. The government overspent that amount by $100 million and this parliament voted that additional sum by way of further supplementary estimates prior to the Easter adjournment.
In order to permit the government to carry on the business of government for a limited period while the house is in session, the house voted two months' interim supply on March 29. This provides the government with sufficient money to transact its business until May 31. When the Minister of Finance asked for that vote of interim supply, he offered the house the usual undertaking which will be found at page 2148 of Hansard. He said:
As I have said, the form of this bill is exactly the same as in previous years, and the passing of the bill does not prejudice the rights and privileges of members of the House of Commons to criticize any of the individual items in the estimates. And I give the usual undertaking that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of passing this interim supply measure.
That customary undertaking is some warrant for the house's proceeding to vote interim supply to the government before it has discharged its proper responsibility of reviewing in detail the proposed estimates of expenditure and also considering by what means the necessary supply is to be raised.
Today the house is being asked to vote an additional four months' interim supply. We have not been told the amount, Mr. Speaker, but we can assume that, on a pro rata basis, it must be approximately $750 million. It might even be a little bit more than that if there are some special items of expenditure to be made prior to September 30.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is about $541 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Parliament will have the right, though.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, this twentieth parliament of Canada is being called upon by the government to assume the responsibility of voting the tidy sum of $541 million, and this parliament knows that it will have no opportunity of discharging its responsibility of reviewing the items of proposed expenditure before it votes that colossal sum of money. It is no answer for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to suggest, as he so glibly suggested yesterday, that it does not matter anyway because the next parliament of Canada, the twenty-first parliament, will have the opportunity of reviewing the estimates. That proposal is an invitation to this twentieth parliament of Canada to abdicate its responsibility. When members of this twentieth parliament are faced with responsibility in connection with the voting of the money of the people-because it is the people's money and not ours-it is no answer to say: Oh well, a later parliament, the twenty-first parliament of Canada, when the government sees fit to call it into session, will have that opportunity. It is this twentieth parliament that is being called upon to vote this colossal sum of money, and it is this twentieth parliament of Canada which must face the responsibility of either voting that amount of money or refusing to do so. If this twentieth parliament simply votes that money without having reviewed the means by which that amount is to be raised, and the ways in which that amount of money is to be spent, I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this twentieth parliament of Canada will go down in history as a par-

llament which turned its back upon its responsibility and abdicated its proper duty to the Canadian people.
You have said that twice.
We will be back.
The hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) says: We will be back. I presume he is talking about himself and myself.
I will be back.

I do not want to be too hard on the hon. member, but I am quite sure that by this time the electors in the riding of Renfrew North will have realized their mistake of 1945 and will set about rectifying it at the earliest opportunity.
You are wrong there.

I have pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that the responsibility for voting this money will rest upon the shoulders of this twentieth parliament, and it is not discharging its responsibility if it says: Oh well, the next parliament, when it comes into session, will have that opportunity. The money will be spent by that time. What is the sense then in talking about the power of parliament to review, when the money is already spent? This parliament in session here and now is the parliament which is going to bear the responsibility for submitting to the demand of the government for this vote of money.
I submit that there is one responsibility, perhaps paramount to all others, which a free parliament cannot lightly reject. The control of parliament over the raising of money and over the expenditure of money has been historically the means by which parliament has exercised its control over the executive branch of the government. It was when parliament in days gone by acquired that exclusive right to decide how money shall be raised and how money shall be spent that parliament won its conflict with monarchical power; and finally when parliament won that exclusive right, it established our present constitutional, parliamentary form of government on a secure foundation. Any departure from that principle of responsibility is a departure that will be taken with grave risk to our whole basis of government.
What does this mean in terms of our responsibility? The government has submitted a volume of estimates embracing 745 items. They total $2,218 million, and with supplementary estimates of $55 million, make a grand total of $2,273 million. If this House of Commons submits to the course that the government is demanding that it take, it simply means that this parliament will have

I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that a government that asks parliament to abdicate its responsibility in that fashion is a government that does not deserve to live.
And it will not.

On the other hand, parliament is not going to be given the opportunity in the limited time that remains of doing its duty with respect to the ways and means of raising the money to provide the supply asked by the government. The government is saying to us in effect: There cannot be any time for the normal consideration of the budget because we have appointed a deadline, and this parliament will die when that deadline is reached. What does the government care about the responsibility of parliament? What do they care about their responsibility to parliament? I do not believe that any such thing exists in their minds. What do they care about our responsibility to the people of Canada, about what parliament is being asked to do today in taking that colossal sum of money belonging to the people of Canada and putting it at the disposal of this government, sir, which has shown such a total lack of responsibility? Sir, this is all of a pattern that has become but too familiar in this House of Commons. Parliamentary government is at stake, and if this House of Commons is to submit meekly to the demands of this government for the voting of this colossal sum by way of interim supply, then I say to you that this twentieth parliament will go down in history as a parliament that has shirked its responsibility.
The third time.

I would be happy, sir, to repeat this simple proposition if I had some hope that it would make some impression upon the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet. It is his misfortune that he entered this parliament during the regime of a government

that has lost all sense of responsibility to parliament. That is the atmosphere in which he has grown up here in these past four years. That is his misfortune. Most of us on the opposition side intend to breathe the clear pure air of responsibility no matter what obstacles are placed in the way by hon. members opposite, who have been invited by this government to treat themselves as so many ciphers, to obey the bidding of their lords on the treasury benches.
This is not the only aspect of the matter, sir, that ought to give this House of Commons reason for thought. We are asked to vote interim supply. The Prime Minister himself does not seem to think that it is necessary, because he undertook to make some comment recently on the subject of governor general's warrants. The house will remember that prior to the Easter recess my colleague, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker), questioned the Minister of Finance as to whether the government considered it lawful to finance its expenditures by the use of governor general's warrants. The Minister of Finance was a little cagey on that occasion and indicated that he was not prepared to give an answer. But in the meantime the government had moved closer to the election and they had carefully investigated all aspects of their supply problem, because when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) arrived in Ottawa last Saturday on his return from his western tour he was met by the press and this question of supply came up. If you please, sir, the Prime Minister informed the press that financial supply could be authorized by governor general's warrants instead of by votes in the House of Commons. That is the statement of the Prime Minister. Why are we here? Sir, we are apparently just going through some motions here, because the government has already decided that whether it gets a vote of interim supply or not, it is going' to spend whatever money it wishes to spend between now and the date on which the new parliament will assemble. Did you ever see, sir, any more bare-faced renunciation of responsibility to parliament, any clearer evidence of the fact that this government has treated parliament, is treating it today as it has treated it hitherto, with studied contempt? This was a carefully calculated statement by the Prime Minister and we may be sure that he made it after due consideration.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance made some extraordinary statements. In effect, he said, "Oh, well, what is the use of taking time to review items of expenditures of $2,200 million, because in my experience of nine years in this house I have never seen anybody move to change any item." The state-

ment is to be found at page 2622 of Hansard. This is what he said:
During all the time that I have been in the house and associated with the Department of Finance, I have never found anyone on the opposition side- and I must say I have never found anyone on my own side-who said that an estimate should be reduced. Let us not try to fool ourselves, even if we are trying to fool the public.
So far as the last sentence is concerned, the Minister of Finance of course can speak for himself, but I wish he would get his facts straight, Mr. Speaker. Instead of bragging about the length of time that he has been in the house, he should just take a little time to get the facts straight before he makes those expansive statements.
May I-

On a point of privilege, I know that my hon. friend wants to be honest with the people in his own riding.
How do you know?
To be fair and decent he should have completed the statement of the Minister of Finance. Read the rest of it.
That was the end of his sentence.
Read it all.

There was an interjection. If the Minister of Labour wants to go on and add another paragraph, let him do it on his own time. I have read the statement of the Minister of Finance, and I am putting the record straight by telling the Minister of Finance that he ought to get his facts straight-

Oh, oh.

If there are shortcomings, and there are grave shortcomings, in the procedure of this house in meeting its responsibility with respect to the review of expenditures, the principal responsibility rests upon the government and, not least of all, upon the shoulders of the Minister of Finance. The means of improving the procedure of this house have been pointed out times without number, and pointed out to the Minister of Finance.
Let me remind the house that on July 9, 1947, the public accounts committee, after having considered this matter and having heard the evidence of the Auditor General himself, made extensive recommendations to the government as to the means of improving the review of estimates and expenditures in this house. The Auditor General pointed out that at the present time so much is crowded into the program of the house that parliament is not doing its duty with respect to the review of expenditures. He said:
-complete examination of estimates is impracticable. Estimates should be presented in such a form that members do not have to guess purposes to which votes will be applied.
That report of the public accounts committee which embodied many recommendations set out the practical way in which this House of Commons could improve the manner in which it undertakes to discharge its responsibility with respect to the review of expenditures. The Auditor General offered recommendations from his long experience and those recommendations were endorsed unanimously by the members of the public accounts committee regardless of party. What has been done?

I doubt very much if the hon. member is correct in saying that the committee endorsed them. The committee has not as yet made its recommendations. There is no report from the public accounts committee.

I wish the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) would wake up and listen to what is going on. I am talking about the report that was made in 1947, when the hon. member was a member of the committee. The hon. member had better listen to what is going on in this house or do his dreaming elsewhere. This report was made to the house by the public accounts committee and it

received the endorsation of every member of that committee, including the hon. member for Halifax.

What action has been taken in connection with these detailed recommendations from the public accounts committee designed to assist parliament in doing its duty? Those recommendations were made to the government. The Liberal members on the committee did not want them made to parliament because there might be a debate that might embarrass the government. In order to be sure of getting them before the house we compromised and agreed that they would be recommendations to the government.
What has this government done in the two intervening years in carrying out these recommendations for improving the method by which parliament could discharge its duty in respect to the review of expenditures? We have the answer, Mr. Speaker, in the strange stony silence from the benches to your right. Nothing has been done. As the Minister of Finance finds in the present procedure an additional reason for inviting parliament to abdicate its responsibilities I say that the responsibility rests upon his shoulders and the shoulders of every member of the government for having done nothing to put into effect those recommendations by the public accounts committee. That is the measure of the sense of responsibility on the part of the moribund government opposite.
There are special reasons why at this session of 1949 parliament should give special attention to these expenditures. I do not intend to review the ground covered by my honourable and esteemed leader in the powerful speech he made this morning, but I do say that it is high time that this parliament lived up to its responsibilities with respect to the use of public money by this government during the lifetime of this parliament. Because of the shortness of time I shall mention only two things among many. First, there are payments for services that were charged before the services were rendered and, second, there were advances made before parliament had authorized them to be made.

P.C. 938 of the same month.

P.C. 1186 of the same month.

That is not very much.

The hon. member for Kings (Mr. Grant) says that that is not much. That is another sample of the mentality of those who occupy the benches opposite. I am reminded of the remark made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) about three years ago on the subject of saving a million dollars in the estimates. The house was reviewing the estimates and when a way was pointed out to save one million the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, "Oh, well, what is a million dollars?" speechtext:

was made last fall in connection with the negotiations with the delegates from Newfoundland. If the Minister of National Health and Welfare does not know that, and does not know that the Prime Minister made that statement, it is high time he did.

Mr. Speaker, during the next ten or fifteen minutes I shall prove to the house that under the present financial regime there is no possibility of assuring our Canadian people security with freedom, because we are working under an antiquated system, and neither the parliament nor the government has any power actually over the financial regime in this country.
To prove what I am saying I shall read opinions given by experts on private money monopoly. In the field of the creation of money-and I see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is laughing; I know that he knows I am right.

Major L. L. B. Angas, in his book "Slump Ahead in Bonds", states:
The modern banking system manufactures money out of nothing. The process is perhaps the most
Financial Policy
astounding piece of sleight of hand that was ever invented. Banks in fact are able to create and cancel modern deposit money. They can in fact inflate, mint and unmint, the modem ledger-entry currency.
Then Robert H. Hemphill, former credit manager of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, says in the foreword of Irving Fisher's book, "100% Money":
If all bank loans were paid, no one would have a bank deposit, and there would not be a dollar of currency or coin in circulation. This is a staggering thought. We are completely dependent on the commercial banks. Someone has to borrow every dollar we have in circulation, cash or credit. If the banks create ample synthetic money, we are prosperous; if not, we starve! We are absolutely without a permanent monetary system.
It is the same in Canada.
When one gets a complete grasp of the picture, the tragic absurdity of our hopeless position is almost incredible-but there it is. It (the banking problem) is the most important subject intelligent persons can investigate and reflect upon. It is so important that our present civilization may collapse unless it is widely understood and the defects remedied very soon.
In Collier's of June 8, 1935, Mr. Eccles, head of the Federal Reserve Board, is quoted as having said this:
The banks can create and destroy money. Bank credit is money. It's the money we do most of our business with, not with that currency which we usually think of as money.
Mr. Irving Fisher, professor emeritus of economics at Yale, says:
When a bank lends or invests, it extends credit, i.e., creates cheque-book money. When it gets loans paid or sells investments, it contracts credit, i.e., destroys cheque-book money. In normal times such creation and destruction of money roughly balance. But when they do not balance the nation's money is inflated or deflated and causes a boom or a depression.
Then, let us take an expert like Thomas Edison, who said:
The only dynamite that works in this country is the dynamite of a sound idea. I think we are getting a sound idea on the money question. The people have an instinct which tells them that something is wrong and that the wrong somehow centers in money.
Don't allow them to confuse you with the cry of "paper money." The danger of paper money is precisely the danger of gold-if you get too much it is no good. There is just one rule for money, and that is to have enough to carry all the legitimate trade that is waiting to move. Too little and too much are both bad. But enough to move trade, enough to prevent stagnation on the one hand and not enough to permit speculation on the other hand, is the proper ratio.
I would ask the Minister of Finance to listen to this and take careful note of it:
If our nation can issue a dollar bond it can issue a dollar bill. The element that makes the bond good makes the bill good also. The difference between the bond and the bill is that the bond lets money brokers collect twice the amount of the bond

Financial Policy
and an additional twenty per cent, whereas the currency pays nobody but those who contribute directly in some useful way.
It is absurd to say that our country can issue $30 million in bonds and not $30 million in currency. Both are promises to pay; but one promise fattens the usurer and the other helps the people.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that before going to the people the Minister of Finance should stand up in this house and enunciate a policy of placing money at the service of the people, thus returning to the parliament of Canada the power of creating credit.
A former president of the United States, Abraham Lincoln, expressed his fear of the bankers' power in what is commonly known as the Lincoln prophecy, which reads as follows:
I see in the near future a crisis arising that unnerves me and causes me to tremble for the safety of my country. As a result of the war, corporations have been enthroned, and an era of corruption in high places will follow until all of liberty shall be lost and the republic destroyed. God grant that my fears may prove groundless.
His fears have been grounded instead.
That great businessman Henry Ford has also observed that:
The function of money is not to make money, but to move goods. Money is only one part of our transportation system. It moves goods from man to man. A dollar bill is like a postage stamp; it is no good unless it will move commodities between persons. If a postage stamp will not carry a letter, or money will not move goods, it is just the same as an engine that will not run. Someone will have to get out and fix it.
I do say, Mr. Speaker, that the only ones who are going out to fix the motor are the Social Crediters.
I have been quoting these men and I should like now to turn to this country and have a look at the conditions existing in Canada. Lately I have seen some pre-election advertisements. On one page of the paper one sees a photograph of the right hon. the Prime Minister and on the next page one sees a photograph of the leader of the opposition. One claims to be saving the country and the other claims to be saving it; both are saving the country. At the same time thousands and thousands of people are starving in Canada. These two gentlemen are saving the people just the same.
Last night I was reading this advertisement featuring a picture of the Prime Minister, a very nice looking man. It is in French and reads as follows:
Our farmers are prosperous under a Liberal government at Ottawa. The Canadian farmers have had a prosperity such as they never saw in the past.
The government issues this only at election time. I never saw this photograph before, not even a year ago. Only when we go to the people to ask for their vote in order to remain in power are we interested in the people.
[Mr. Caouette.l

That may be true but the story does not end there.
It says here that:
The Liberal government has given security to the farmers.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I would say that the security of the Canadian people lies with the Canadian people and not with the government. The Canadian people have no security, actually, but the party politicians have a kind of security which is based on the people's lack of knowledge. I would say they are not truthful with the people. They will say that the farmers have an income three times higher than in 1939 but they do not say, of course, that the whole Dominion of Canada is producing today $15 billion a year, while in 1939 the total production amounted to about $5-5 billion. This amount was not produced by the government, but by the Canadian people.
These people do not say in their advertisement that our national debt has increased not merely three times, but much more than that. In 1939 our national debt amounted to $3,710,610,592.87. It was $3 billion in 1939, while in 1948 our national debt amounted to $17 billion. The figure three has been multiplied by nearly six. We say our farmers have an income three times higher than in 1939 while our debt is six times higher than it was.
The total interest paid on our national debt since the confederation of Canada amounts to $5,743,769,052. We cannot find money for our old age pensioners, but we pay $5 billion in interest. We may say we have increased the pension to $40 at the age of seventy, but what are we doing for the aged

who are between sixty and seventy? We have no money. Only the Social Crediters in this house are complaining about the money paid to the financiers of this country, to the controllers of our economic blood- money.
Then we find that the revenue collected in the form of taxes by the Department of National Revenue, that department which digs into the pockets of our people, amounted to $502,171,353 in 1939 and in 1948 it amounted to nearly $3 billion. Again, if you multiply it out you find that we are taxing the people six times more today than we were nine years ago. Yet, we tell the people of Canada that they have prosperity such as they never had in the past.
There is one matter to which I would draw the attention of the house. In 1913, before the first war, our national debt was $483 million. In 1920, after the war, our national debt was $3 billion. In 1930, before the depression, our national debt was $2,500 million. In 1939, after the depression, at the start of world war II, our national debt was $3,710 million. We were not able to find money at that time to establish peace and to secure liberty with security for all our people. While in 1939 our national debt was $3 billion, in 1948 it stood at $17 billion. To fight a war we found $14 billion, while during peacetime we could not find money in Canada. We would not go to the banks to borrow because we said that would increase the debt, and that we should not go into debt like that during that time. But when the war comes, with Christians fighting against Christians, we find money. But nowhere in Canada can we find it when it is time to establish peace for all and to establish a social justice which would guarantee to every citizen of this country security with freedom and also to help our aged, for whom I again ask a pension of $60 at the age of 60 without any means test.
I am asking for consideration for the cripples in Canada. Today there is no chance for them. We are treating animals better than we are treating our cripples who, after all, are human beings just as you and I are, Mr. Speaker, and as are all hon. members of this house. We cannot find money for them. There is no chance for them. Yet when we ask for a national dividend, we are laughed at. Some people find it funny. They say that Social Crediters are only talking about money. Money is not so important, they say; but money is of great importance, Mr. Speaker. We know that money power controls this government. We know that money power controls the Canadian government and all the ministers of the Canadian government.

I have here a pamphlet entitled Economic Liberalism written by Reverend Father Gerard Petit, c.s.c.
We have stated over and over again that communism is nothing more than the legitimate offspring of economic liberalism. Now, to show what is understood by this term, I wish to point out its main shortcomings which are set forth in this little tract.
The first fault of economic liberalism is selfishness.
The Liberal system certainly reeks of selfishness, and I must draw the attention of the house to the fact that economic liberalism is doomed to oblivion because it is rotten with selfishness. It is for this reason that His Holiness Pope Pius XI, in his encyclical Quadragesimo Anno, stated that economic liberalism was tainted with egotism. His Holiness also denounced:
That nefarious individualism that overlooks the social and moral character of economic life, that selfishness which seeks only its own profit and results in so unfair a distribution of wealth.
That is a cause of communism.
If the first error of economic liberalism is to make selfishness the primary motive of the economic body's operation:
The second is to urge people to produce rather than to serve. It is a consequence of the first error. Since they are concerned only with material wellbeing, disregarding the rules of ethics as extraneous considerations, they come to the point where they seek to produce as much as possible in order to get rich as quickly as possible. The worker is made subordinate to his machine and to the manufactured product, the consumer is swept by the torrent of frenzied competition and the interests of the producers. It is, it has been said, the manufactured article that controls the man who has made it.
It is the manufactured product that creates the need. It is competition that partly regulates wages.

And now, Mr. Speaker, here is the third error of the Liberal system, of economic liberalism.
Liberalism worships a false god, a golden calf. It is this modern idol, this awful power with its international ramifications that can hold political authority in check, plunge humanity into wars and revolutions and throw into confusion the lives of individuals and of nations.
It is here that His Holiness Pope Pius XI denounces this control over our economic life blood.
Economic liberalism gives rise to communism. Before outlawing communism in Canada or elsewhere we should see to it that the present Liberal regime in Canada is outlawed itself. I say that today in Canada two courses are open to us: communism on the one side and social credit on the other. There is no alternative. Either parliament will adopt the social credit policy in economic and social matters or, whether we want it or not, we shall experience the same consequences, the same troubles that Europe is experiencing today. During the election campaign which will start in a few days and which will end with the vote of June 27, we shall hear many statements and many noble speeches. I ask

Government Policies
our friends of the Liberal party that they explain to the province of Quebec and to the country, during that campaign, why so far Canada has not appointed an ambassador or a representative to the Vatican. We note and observe throughout the world that Great Britain, for example, is represented at the Vatican; so is the United States, as well as European countries, while Canada which claims to be a Christian country has not deemed fit to appoint a representative to the Vatican. Is that logical? I wish that during the election campaign someone would explain to the Canadian people why we have not yet appointed an ambassador to the Vatican.
Then I wish someone would tell us why the government and parliament have not as yet deemed fit to adopt a distinctive flag for our country, a flag which would make us known throughout the world as a sovereign, free and independent nation.
I wish to mention a third point. The matter of a national anthem has been discussed in the house lately and it was suggested that "O Canada" be recognized as such. May I take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote) for having introduced a resolution to that effect and I consider as enemies of their country those who are opposed to the adoption of "O Canada" as our national anthem. All true Canadians favour the adoption of a national anthem for Canada.
I said a moment ago that the Social Credit party had a solution for the present-day problems. The only thing Canada now lacks for ensuring security and freedom to her citizens is purchasing power.
Much is said about compulsory health insurance, contributory old age pensions, and so forth. Contributions are not what will give us security with freedom. When the qualifying word "compulsory" is appended to a pension or to any social legislation, it is no longer freedom but servitude or dictatorship.
We want security with freedom. The means to achieve it is to put purchasing power in the hands of consumers, so that they may arrange their lives themselves. They could thus obtain the useful goods or the land and houses they need. In that way we would guarantee them security with liberty.
The cart should not be put before the horse, as is now the case. Let the government assume once again control as regards the emission and circulation of money in this country, let them increase the purchasing power in proportion with the real needs of the people. It will then be sufficient to take [Mr. Caouette.l
care of production. The Canadian people will have security with freedom and their way of life will be more in keeping with Christian principles.
For three years, I have represented the riding of Pontiac in this house. After the next election, I will represent the riding of Villeneuve.
I have not been elected merely to discuss the present system, but to wage the real fight of the Canadian people and more particularly of the electors of my county. Mr. Speaker, in this morning's Montreal Gazette there was a reference to a brief which had been submitted to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) by the Canadian Exporters Association, in which there was a charge that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had misled the public regarding the trade situation of Canada. I think this is the time when this matter should be discussed because, of the interim supply, a minimum of $27 million is desired for the next four months to carry on the Department of Trade and Commerce. In the brief, which was evidently given to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the government was also charged with allowing a further deterioration in the trade of the dominion.
The continued deterioration of Canada's export trade position is a matter of grave concern to this nation and one which demands immediate action by the government, action which should be taken before parliament is dissolved, possibly tomorrow. Unfortunately the government has chosen to defer dealing with this vital question in the hope that the election will be over before the people of Canada as a whole fully realize the serious situation with which they are now faced because of inaction and blundering by the Department of Trade and Commerce with their do-nothing policy as far as trade is concerned.
The government policy of leaning on the United States, because that is what we have done in the last few months, on the European recovery program, the Atlantic pact, and any other prop which may be available to the government at this time, has put us in the position in which we are today. In an effort to hide the true situation the publicity bureau

of the Department of Trade and Commerce is working overtime to tell the Canadian people about our increased exports to the United States, and how these were made possible by the actions of the present government. What they fail to mention, however, is the temporary nature of these exports, a situation which is rapidly being realized today as surpluses are expected in United States production.
The history of trade in the past has shown that, because of similarity of production in the United States and Canada, the Canadian producer always loses the United States markets as soon as they have an excess of supplies available in that country. Speakers, in an effort to justify the trade policy of this floundering government, have stated that export trade in 1948 has set a new peacetime record in dollar value. What they fail to tell the Canadian people is that this was due to expenditures of ECA money, and other moneys which the United States government made available for this purpose. They are relying on that more than they are on a sound or reasonable dependence upon United States markets, which take too great a percentage of their imports from this country in raw, unprocessed materials. As a result of misleading government propaganda, the Canadian people are not fully aware of the danger which today threatens their export markets.
I was very pleased today, as I was yesterday, to hear the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) deal with this subject. He treated it more from the point of view of agriculture than I propose to do at this time. As surpluses accumulate in the United States, and the indications are very definite that such surpluses are appearing there, Canadian export markets will be further restricted. Our export outlets to the United Kingdom have been lost largely because of the inadequacy of the government in dealing with situations as they arise from day to day. They have a tendency to drift along any course except that of facing up to the problem in line with their responsibilities as a government.
During the period 1939 to 1949 we negotiated 142 contracts with the United Kingdom for the supply of various foodstuffs, and had as many as twenty-two of these in effect at one time. Today we have three contracts left. Those other markets for primary products of the producers of this country have been lost to such countries as Russia, Poland, the Ukraine, Hungary, Denmark, Yugoslavia, Roumania, and many others that are too numerous to name.
It was mentioned in the house last night by the hon. member for Lake Centre that the
Trade
chief issue in the coming election will be the trade policy of the government. As one who represents an urban riding, where there are many factories, I certainly agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I subscribe to that view wholeheartedly because in this nation one-third of our national income is derived from our export trade, and I think everybody will agree that our export trade is being seriously threatened today by the wholly inadequate policies and efforts of the present government.
The hon. member for Lake Centre pointed out to the house this afternoon that two days ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce told the people of Canada that there was nothing to worry about as far as our trade was concerned, and that he was going to England, not to try to obtain trade, or to seek agreements, but to open the trade fair. The hon. member for Lake Centre also pointed out that in today's Canadian newspapers there appeared a statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce made in England to Reuters news agency, I believe, that his main reason for being in England was to obtain trade for this country.
In the month of February our favourable balance of trade with the rest of the world slumped sharply when it fell from $15,200,000 in January to $1,200,000 in February. For the same month last year our favourable trade balance was $28,100,000. These figures indicate clearly the present trend in our trade relations and speak in no uncertain terms of the reason the government hopes to get a snap election over with before the effects become widely known and felt by the citizens of this country as a whole.
The effect, Mr. Speaker, of this present trend in our trade, if allowed to continue, will mean in the next three months that where three men were employed in a factory in Canada one man will be left in employment. It will mean accumulated surpluses in the hands of primary producers of this country. Farmers will again be called upon to be the shock absorbers to a recession in our economy. There is no question about it that if this situation continues in the way it is today our farmers will have surplus farm products, our miners will have a surplus of base metals and, going right through the piece, our manufacturers will have a surplus of manufactured products.
Surplus production on the one hand and government policies resulting in loss of markets on the other means difficult days ahead not only for Canadian farmers but for Canadian industry and Canadian workers as a whole.
No one knows better the truth of the present situation I have just described than

Trade
the ministers of the government, and more particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I believe he is a little late in his desire or his ambition to go to the old country and to Europe to try to regain some of those lost markets which, I suggest, we lost through carelessness on the part of the department which handles these affairs.
The present loss of markets to Canada, arising largely because of the policy of the present government to depend upon the action of other governments, and their failure to take any constructive action themselves not only threatens to bring about a national crisis in this country in a matter of a few months, but threatens the very basis of our whole social security program.
While on the one hand the government talks of all the social security measures it proposes for the people of Canada, its policies of inaction, floundering and failure are losing marke.s which, in the past, have accounted for one-third of the national income of this nation. If we are to be in a position to pay for these social security measures, which every party in this house believes are most desirable, then we must maintain our export trade as a means of financing such social security programs.
Without maximum employment and maximum revenue from taxation, the old age pension which was passed yesterday, and many others of these social security policies, could not be brought into effect. The only alternative, if we cannot maintain our trade, is to finance such a program by excessive taxation-and we have seen something of excessive taxation in this country. It is only with the budget of this year that taxes have been reduced to a point where people do not find it so hard to pay them. The type of excessive taxation to which we have been subjected in the last few years has been a very heavy burden upon the people of this country.
Our volume of exports this year, to date, is much less than it was for corresponding months last year. Much more serious, however, is the fact that the reduced value of orders now on hand-and I think hon. members should understand this-is reflecting itself in a continuing downward trend week by week; and indications are it will become increasingly serious within a matter of some months, unless positive measures are taken immediately to halt the decline in our export markets.
Notwithstanding the apparent hurry of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to close off discussion in this parliament relating to matters of vital concern to the country, there are several aspects of the present government's policy upon which the Canadian people are entitled to further information. I
[Mr. Cockeram.)
propose to place on the records of parliament at this time several of these urgent questions pertaining to government policy on matters of trade, and I would ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of Trade and Commerce to provide parliament and the Canadian people with the information requested before calling for dissolution.
My questions are these:
1.	Under the provisions of the Atlantic pact, and in accordance with the statement of the Prime Minister on November 11 last that in the opinion of the Canadian government the Atlantic pact would not be fully effective if it is nothing more than a military alliance, but must concern itself with matters of trade as well, what representations, if any, have been made by Canada to-
(a) Instigate immediate discussions among countries presently signatories to the Atlantic pact, with a view towards discontinuance of the present trend of self-isolation in matters of trade through the medium of barter deals, particularly with countries within or under the shadow of the iron curtain?
I believe this is a very important question. We have signed the Atlantic pact, and if any discussion took place, then certainly trade matters were discussed. I say the government should say where we are heading in this regard.
2.	What representations if any have been made by the Canadian government with a view towards removal of the barriers to trade within the signatory nations of the Atlantic pact, particularly with reference to the dollar-sterling situation?
3.	What representations if any have been made by the Canadian government relative to the continued departure, by countries signatory to the Atlantic pact, from the expressed purpose of multilateral trade, as outlined in the Geneva and Havana trade agreements to which Canada and these other countries are also signatories?
4.	What representations if any have been made by the Canadian government to the government of the United Kingdom for the purpose of reviewing under present circumstances the disastrous effect upon Canada's present and future trade arising from the imposition of the present fiscal policy of the United Kingdom in matters of trade upon her colonies, which are members of the British commonwealth of nations, to which Canada belongs?

when parliament opened to have been meeting in London at that time, and reported in the press to have adjourned about a week later.
I bring these questions to the attention of the government because the people I represent-and I represent an urban riding-as well as the Canadian people as a whole want to know the position of the government in these matters.
The man who works in a factory is vitally interested because he knows that today orders are rapidly falling off because of our inability to export, and that unless some positive action is taken now he will be receiving a notice in his pay envelope that his services are to be discontinued.
Farmers know that unless markets are found for their products surpluses will accumulate, prices will fall to levels below cost, and their standard of living will be reduced accordingly.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, before this parliament dissolves the people of Canada are entitled to further information as to the trade policies of the government. The people should be told what action, if any, is to be taken to meet the present serious crisis arising in this country.

Why, since 1930, when its commercial possibilities were confirmed in the findings of the senior geologist of the mines department, did the federal government fail to assist in developing the Wilberforce uranium deposits while at the same time paying excessively high mining and recovery costs at the Eldorado mine?
The government has spent over $60 million at Eldorado and it is a well-known fact that Eldorado is petering out. It is well-known that the government is engaged in a frantic search for more uranium in that area in order to justify the expenditure in that place. At the same time we are satisfied, not only by the government's report that has been hidden, but by other geologists from the

United States, that there is a great ore body of uranium in the Wilberforce area.
Why, in the face of the Spence report, have both the federal government and the atomic energy control board refused to acknowledge the existence of the Wilberforce uranium resources? Since examination and confirmation of the uranium resources of the Wilberforce area by agents of the atomic energy control board in 1947, headed by Dr. Fortier, why has the government flatly refused to make the results of their findings available to the private enterprise that put up the money to finance that operation? There is no doubt in my mind and there is no doubt in the government's mind or in the minds of any of the atomic energy commission that we have been and are breaking into a time of atomic energy. We need this available energy and power of all descriptions in peacetime. We may need it in wartime, but God forbid that we should. I hope we never do. At the same time the way to avoid war is to be ready for it. It has been proved that we need atomic energy. I think it is high time that this government gave the Wilberforce area some consideration or told us why they will not give it consideration. That area is within one hundred miles of their atomic energy plant. It is within one hundred miles of their Port Hope plant. I should like to know why it has not received some consideration, or why we cannot get some information, or why the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) flatly refused to give us information with regard to a report that was financed by the people of that area, not by a company or by a stockselling scheme, because we know that atomic energy and uranium are controlled by the government. Saint John Harbour Bridge

speechtext:
This motion, Mr. Speaker, enables me to bring to the attention of the government a grievance that many people in my constituency have put up with for a good many years. It would be perhaps more correct for me to call this an inconvenience rather than a grievance. It has to do with the fact that there is no bridge across the harbour of Saint John connecting the west part of the city with the east part of the city. A bridge of this kind has been needed for many years. In fact, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett proposed to construct this bridge. He had already rebuilt the docks and the elevators at west Saint John after a most disastrous fire but he was prevented from going on with this work by the world-wide depression which took place at about that time and continued for a good many years.
At the present time the connection between the east and the west side of the harbour is provided either by a ferry boat, which is inconvenient, or by a rather long roundabout route that crosses the bridge over the Reversing falls at the mouth of the river St. John and then passes through the parish of Lancaster to the west side of the city.
It is my purpose tonight to advocate the construction of this bridge. This bridge would shorten the distance between the west part of the city, where most of the ocean docks and terminals are situated, and the eastern part of the city where most of the business of the community is carried on. It would help to develop the freight business of the Canadian National Railways. It would be a matter of great convenience to the residents and the port workers who reside in both parts of the city, and it would help promote the business interests of the community.
The cost of such a bridge, it has been estimated recently by a reliable engineer, would be about $3,500,000. I regard $3,500,000 as a lot of money. I have never advocated in this house the spending of the taxpayers' money unless I have been convinced that the expenditure is justified on economic grounds, or that it is for the general good of Canada. But from the inquiries I have made I have come to the conclusion that this bridge would pay for itself if tolls were imposed for its use.
At the present time the Canadian National Railways pay forty cents per ton to switch their freight from their terminals on the eastern side of the harbour over the Canadian Pacific Railway bridge that crosses the mouth of the river to the docks and terminals in west Saint John. I am informed that the Canadian National Railways handle approximately 300,000 tons of freight a year. I am informed that a Canadian National Railways
2714	HOUSE OF
Saint John Harbour Bridge traffic expert has stated that if the harbour bridge were constructed the freight tonnage on the Canadian National Railways would be doubled in about five years.
The town planning commission of the city of Saint John made a traffic count last month and found 5,972 vehicles in one day passed to and fro between west Saint John and east Saint John or Saint John proper. These trucks and cars would in the ordinary course of events use this bridge if it were constructed.
At the present time the city of Saint John is losing about $75,000 a year in the operation of the ferry boat which crosses the harbour, and it will not be long before it will be necessary for the city to construct a new boat at a cost of about $500,000.
Then the transportation company of the city-that is the company which runs the buses between Saint John and west Saint John-could get along with three buses less than they use at the present time if the bridge were built and the long roundabout route it is forced to use now was eliminated. The company says that it costs between $15,000 and $18,000 a year to operate one of these buses.
What does all this add up to? If the figures that I have been given are correct, as I have reason to believe they are, it means that a bridge that would cost $3,500,000 would pay for itself.
Let me give the figures. First, as to the annual charges: interest at 3J per cent on $3,500,000 would amount to $122,000. Maintenance at 1 per cent would amount to $35,000. Depreciation at 2 per cent would amount to $70,000. Therefore the total annual charges would be $227,000.
As to the revenues, if the Canadian National Railways used this bridge to the extent of hauling 600,000 tons of freight-and that is the estimated amount within a few years- at twenty cents a ton, the revenue would amount to $120,000. Tolls from motor vehicles and passengers are estimated to amount to $200,000. Tolls from the bus company would amount to $30,000, and the annual deficit which the city has now on its ferry is $75,000. These amounts total $425,000.
I think these figures are arresting and deserving of a great deal of attention. If they are approximately correct, and I have received them from reliable sources, then the building of this bridge would be amply justified. My suggestion is that the government guarantee the bonds of the national harbours board in an amount sufficient for the construction of this bridge after it has checked my figures and entered into fair arrangements with the parties who are interested. I urge


strongly that this be done. The matter has been long delayed. If the figures I have given are about right then there is no reason why the building of this bridge should be further delayed. In fact it is of importance that the work be commenced at the earliest possible moment.
